abstract: Although methods for the electrical transmission of sound frequencies have been in existence for a long time, it is only in recent years that the transmission of high quality music and speech has received serious attention. When the power of radio transmitters was continually increased it became desirable to have the studios and transmitting stations a wide distance apart, since the transmitter was best situated outside a city, white the studio should most conveniently remain in a central position. Also, interconnection between one central studio and a number of transmitters scattered all over the country, necessitated by simultaneous broadcasting of important events, requires an efficient system of land lines. It was found that ordinary telephone lines did not fulfil requirements as to quality.

articleTitle: Who has the largest output?
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Whilst discussing the rising load curve the other day, somebody asked us what British electric supply undertaking had the largest output. On the spur of the moment we said that it was the Victoria Falls and Transvaal Power Co., but then we remembered Niagara. Perhaps we should not include Niagara in the story because, although there are 1.6 million horse-power installed, this power is not all developed by any one concern. Pending receipt of the inevitable letter which swoops down like a buzzard on any claims for a record, we shall tentatively submit the Victoria Falls as a winner. In their last financial year they generated nearly 2,000 million units (1,985,883,567), and sold 1,048,148,617. This even leaves the London Power Company behind; they sold 1,474,974,529 units last year. The County of London Company sold a mere trifle of 1,050,835,517 units.

articleTitle: Lightning discharge research in South Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers often contain matter of great practical value. In Vol. XXVII, Part I, there is a report by Professor B. F. J. Schonland on the records of the Lightning Research Committee. It has been said by competent authorities that this is the most important contribution to the study of lightning since the days of Benjamin Franklin. South Africa has a bounteous supply of such phenomena. The Committee are well informed of research in other parts of the world, such as the experiments of the American General Electric, to which we referred, not long ago, and the various radio investigations into atmospherics and lightning discharge, but their work goes beyond all this. Professor Schonland exhibits a sort of general picture, which is the outcome of one hundred and twenty photographic studies made with the Boys camera, which gives the equivalent of two million shots of the lightning discharge per second. It is a fascinating description well worth reading, lint photographic research, he says, is only part of the story. Although it gives us useful evidence and leads to some interesting deductions, the Committee is not content with observing luminosity produced by the flash. The electrical changes occurring before and during the discharge are now being investigated by the cathode-ray oscillograph, and it is hoped to solve the problem of the nature and genesis of a flash. The processes which precede an ordinary spark breakdown are so rapid that observation is extremely difficult; in the lightning discharge they occupy about a thousand times as long, and they are comparatively easy to note. This, it is suggested, may have an important incidence on the design and testing of electrical equipment.

articleTitle: The measurement of lightning voltages and currents on a 40 Kv transmission line
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper gives a preliminary account of an investigation being undertaken on one of the 40 kV transmission lines of the Victoria Falls and Transvaal Power Company, Ltd. The object of the work is to measure, by means of a cathode ray oscillograph and klydonograph, the wave shape and amplitude of overvoltages produced on the line by lightning strokes discharging near it or directly on to it. In addition, a number of magnetic links used in conjunction with a surge crest ammeter have been installed on the masts of the line in order to measure the lightning currents flowing to earth. Certain masts are also equipped with lightning stroke indicators to show the number of times a mast is struck during a storm. The apparatus used is described in detail and special features of the equipment are noted.

abstract: The Council is empowered each year at its discretion to award the Gold Medal of the Institute, together with a certificate and, if considered desirable, a premium not exceeding £10 10s., to a member of any grade for an original paper of outstanding merit submitted during the year.
